blocks.text: Mark carefully distributes responsibility across the chapter: priestly leaders accuse Jesus, the crowd calls for Barabbas, Pilate authorizes the sentence, and Roman soldiers carry out the mockery and crucifixion. The repeated title “King of the Jews” frames both the accusation and the soldiers’ ridicule. The women who watch the death and burial are also active witnesses in the narrative, not incidental observers.

Mark preserves and translates Semitic expressions at key moments. Here he explains Golgotha as “the place of a skull” and translates Jesus’ cry, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” The translation makes the cry available to readers while the retained wording gives particular force to the misunderstanding of bystanders who think Jesus is calling Elijah.

The narrative distinguishes the public execution from what follows: the centurion confirms Jesus’ death, Pilate releases the body to Joseph, Joseph wraps it in linen and places it in a rock-cut tomb, and two women see where he is laid. An archaeological find from an early Roman Jerusalem tomb—an iron nail through a heel bone—shows that at least one crucified person received Jewish tomb burial. It does not establish Jesus’ burial, but it cautions against treating such burial as impossible.
